lines.text:
The Open Stage — Life on the Savanna

The savanna is the most visible ecosystem on Earth. Unlike a forest, where life hides behind canopy and undergrowth, the savanna displays everything. The grassland stretches to the horizon, and every animal — predator and prey — is visible across the open plain. This visibility has made the African savanna the world's most filmed, most photographed, and most visited wild landscape.

The terrain is defined by space and light. Grassland dominates — golden in the dry season, green after the rains. An acacia tree — flat-topped and thorny — is the savanna's signature plant. A baobab — a massive, swollen-trunked tree that stores water — can live for thousands of years. A termite mound — a towering structure of hardened earth — rises from the plain like a clay skyscraper. A watering hole draws every species during the dry months. The horizon is unbroken for kilometres. A sunset paints the sky in orange, red, and violet. A dry riverbed fills only during the rainy season. A kopje — a rocky outcrop — provides shelter and high ground. Dust rises behind every moving herd.

The large mammals are the savanna's spectacle. A lion — the apex predator — hunts in coordinated groups called prides. An elephant — the largest land animal — reshapes the landscape by pushing over trees. A giraffe — the tallest — browses leaves no other animal can reach. A zebra's stripes may confuse predators when the herd moves. A hippo spends the day submerged in water. A rhino — critically endangered — is heavily protected. A buffalo forms defensive herds of hundreds. A cheetah — the fastest land animal — sprints at over a hundred kilometres per hour. A leopard hunts alone and drags its prey into trees. A wildebeest undertakes the largest land migration on Earth, crossing rivers and plains in herds of millions.

Smaller mammals fill ecological niches. A meerkat stands upright as a sentinel, scanning the sky for eagles. A warthog trots with its tail raised. A mongoose hunts snakes. A hyena — often misunderstood — is an efficient scavenger and hunter. A jackal patrols the edges of larger kills. A baboon lives in complex social groups. A gazelle and an impala are the prey species most frequently hunted.

Birds are abundant. An ostrich — the largest bird, flightless — runs across the plain. A vulture circles above a carcass. A flamingo gathers at alkaline lakes. An eagle hunts from height. A stork wades in shallow water. A weaver bird constructs elaborate hanging nests. A hornbill perches in an acacia. A secretary bird stamps on snakes. A guinea fowl moves in noisy groups. A kingfisher and a crane inhabit the wetter zones. A heron fishes at the water's edge.

Safari tourism makes the savanna accessible. A jeep carries visitors along dirt tracks. Binoculars bring distant animals close. A camera captures the experience. A guide interprets animal behaviour and identifies tracks in the dust. A tent and a campfire provide overnight accommodation. A ranger ensures safety and conservation. A map navigates the reserve. A sunhat protects from equatorial sun.

The ecological vocabulary is essential. A predator hunts. Prey is hunted. A herd is a group of herbivores. Migration is seasonal movement — driven by rain and grass. Drought — an extended period without rain — reshapes behaviour and survival. The rainy season restores the grassland. The food chain connects grass to herbivore to predator. Camouflage conceals. Territory is defended. A den shelters young.

The savanna is a landscape of relationships — every species connected to every other by what it eats, what eats it, and where the water is. To understand the savanna is to understand ecology at its most visible and dramatic.

lines.text: In safari tourism, 'the Big Five' refers to five iconic African animals: lion, elephant, buffalo, leopard, and rhinoceros. The term originally came from big-game hunting (the five most difficult animals to hunt on foot) but is now used for wildlife watching and photography.

lines.text: 'Safari' = a Swahili word meaning 'journey'. 'Game drive' = a vehicle tour to see wildlife. 'Game reserve' = a protected area for wildlife. 'Bush' = the wild, uncultivated area (going 'into the bush'). 'Lodge' = safari accommodation. 'Ranger' = a guide or park officer.

lines.text: Both spellings are correct. 'Savanna' (one h) is more common in scientific/geographical texts. 'Savannah' (double h) is more common as a place name (e.g. Savannah, Georgia, USA). In British English, both are used. The word comes from the Taino language (Caribbean).

lines.text: 'Wildlife' is uncountable — always singular: 'the wildlife is', 'wildlife was.' Never *'wildlife are.' For plural reference, use 'wild animals': 'The wild animals are incredible.' Similarly: 'livestock is' (collective singular). Note: 'a lion, elephants, and giraffes' are countable individuals, but 'wildlife' as a category is uncountable.

lines.text: Modal verbs (can, could, will, would, must, should, may, might) + bare infinitive — no 's', no 'to': 'can run', 'must hunt', 'should protect.' Never *'can runs.' The modal carries the tense and person; the main verb stays in base form. 'She can run' (not *she can runs). 'They must leave' (not *they must to leave).

lines.text: 'Despite' + noun/gerund: 'despite the severe drought', 'despite being exhausted.' 'Although' + clause: 'although the drought was severe.' Never *'despite + subject + verb.' 'In spite of' follows 'despite': 'in spite of the drought.' This remains one of the most persistent errors at B2 level.

lines.text: 'Each' + singular verb: 'Each has.' 'Each of the animals has...' The subject is 'each' (singular), not 'animals' (plural). Compare: 'All of the animals have...' Using 'its' with 'each' is grammatically precise; 'their' is accepted in informal usage for gender neutrality but 'its' is standard for animals.

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable: 'fewer species', 'fewer animals.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less danger', 'less poaching', 'less habitat loss.' 'Species' is both singular and plural (same form): 'one species is' / 'many species are.' Since species can be counted, use 'fewer.' Watch for context: 'less wildlife' (uncountable) but 'fewer wild animals' (countable).
